Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world's largest contract chipmaker, founded in 1987 in Hsinchu, Taiwan. Its founder Morris Chang, a veteran of Texas Instruments, was invited by the Taiwanese government to build a chip industry.

TSMC's idea was the "pure-play foundry": it makes chips designed by other companies and sells none under its own name. This let firms such as Apple, Nvidia and AMD design chips without building their own plants, which cost billions of dollars each.

By the 2020s TSMC made most of the world's most advanced chips, the ones in phones, computers and AI systems. That makes Taiwan central to the world economy, and its "silicon shield" is often named in talk about China and Taiwan. It has begun to build plants in Arizona, Japan and Germany. Its main rival in the most advanced chips is South Korea's Samsung.
